text.en:
Nisha kept two bean seeds in two pots. One pot was in the sun and the other in a dark cupboard. She gave both the same water.
After ten days the pot in the sun had a taller, green plant.
"Sunlight helps plants grow," she wrote in her notebook.

Science starts with curiosity: we notice something and ask a question, such as "Does a plant need light?"
We make a guess called a hypothesis, then test it with an experiment. In a fair test we change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
We observe and record what happens, using our senses and tools such as a ruler or thermometer, and write it in a notebook or a table.
From the records we draw a conclusion. If the result does not match our guess, that is fine. We learn from it and try again.
Scientists share what they find so that others can check it. Honesty and patience are important in science.
Science begins when we notice something and ask a question.
We make a guess, then test it. In a fair test we change only one thing.
We observe and write down what happens. We must record honestly.
Then we draw a conclusion and share it. If the guess was wrong, we learn and try again.

problem.en: Nisha tests whether plants need light. What should she keep the same in both pots?

text.en: She changes only one thing: the light.

why.en: A fair test changes one thing.

text.en: So she keeps the water, soil, seed and pot size the same.
Then any difference in growth is because of light.

prompt.en: A friend tests two seeds, one in sun with lots of water and one in the dark with little water. Why is this not a fair test?

requiredIdeas.en: More than one thing is different: light and water.
We cannot tell which one caused the change.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking you can change many things at once.

points.en: A fair test changes only one thing.
We record observations honestly and draw a conclusion.
